opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one of the hardest parts of the work. "Do no harm" sounds simple, but in practice almost every interesting medical question involves trade-offs. If a model refuses to engage with someone asking about medication dosages, that might feel "safe," but it can also leave a person without information they genuinely need, maybe at two in the morning when they can't reach a doctor. So unhelpfulness is itself a form of harm, and we try to take that seriously.

The way I think about translating principles into behavior has a few layers.

First, you have to be concrete about what harm actually looks like in context. That means working closely with physicians across specialties and geographies. A lot of the judgment calls are subtle: when should the model escalate and say "you need to go to an emergency department now," versus helping someone understand their symptoms and options? Clinicians have intuitions about this built from years of practice, and we want to capture them explicitly rather than guess.

Second, you need evaluations that reflect realistic use, not just multiple-choice exam questions. Models have basically saturated those benchmarks, and they don't tell you much about whether a model behaves well in a messy, real conversation where the user is anxious, missing context, or describing something ambiguous. So we've invested in rubric-based evaluation, where physicians write detailed criteria for what a good response looks like in a specific scenario: Did it ask the right clarifying questions? Did it flag the red-flag symptoms? Did it hedge appropriately without being uselessly vague? That turns a fuzzy principle into thousands of specific, checkable behaviors.

Third, context-seeking matters a lot. A good doctor doesn't answer the first question literally; they figure out who they're talking to and what's actually going on. We want models to do the same: recognize when they're missing crucial information and ask for it, and tailor responses depending on whether they're talking to a worried parent or a clinician looking for a quick reference.

And finally, it's iterative. You ship, you learn from how people actually use these systems, you find failure modes you didn't anticipate, and you update both the specifications and the evaluations. The principle stays the same, but your understanding of what it requires keeps getting sharper.

So in a sense, "do no harm" becomes less a rule and more a commitment to keep measuring carefully, against real clinical judgment, whether the model is actually making people's health outcomes better.

r001.rationale: The response describes explicit, checkable criteria, but does not say these specifications make behavior transparent.

r002.rationale: It says “do no harm” involves trade-offs and that specific judgments depend on context, so the principle alone does not determine the model’s behavior.

r003.rationale: It proposes working with physicians across specialties and geographies, but does not specify collective expertise from hundreds of physicians.

r004.rationale: It explains that physician-written evaluation rubrics turn a broad principle into specific, checkable behaviors.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that "do no harm" on its own doesn't tell you very much. It's a principle that everyone agrees with, and that's kind of the problem. If you take it too literally, the safest model is one that refuses to say anything about health at all, and that's clearly a bad outcome. People are already coming to these models with real questions, often because they can't get a doctor on the phone, or they left an appointment confused, or they're trying to make sense of a lab result at eleven at night. Refusing to help them isn't neutral. It has a cost too.

So the way I think about it is you have to decompose the principle into the actual situations where it gets tested. What should the model do when someone describes symptoms that could be an emergency? What should it do when someone asks about a medication interaction? What should it do when someone asks about a diagnosis their doctor already gave them and they just want to understand it better? Each of those has a different right answer, and the right answer depends a lot on context, on who's asking, and on how confident the model can actually be.

One frame that's been useful for us is to ask what a really good clinician would do in that situation, not a defensive one. A good doctor doesn't refuse to engage. They help you understand what's going on, they're honest about uncertainty, and they know when to say, this is the kind of thing where you need to be seen in person, or you need to go to the ER right now. That's the behavior you want. Helpful by default, direct about what it doesn't know, and very clear about escalation when the stakes are high.

The second piece, and I think this is where a lot of the real work is, is that you can't just write that down and hope the model does it. You need to measure it. We've spent a lot of time building evaluations with physicians where we take realistic conversations and ask, did the model get the facts right, did it appropriately recommend care when it should have, did it avoid being alarmist when it shouldn't have, did it communicate in a way the person can actually act on. Those evaluations are where the principle becomes concrete, because you're forced to say what good looks like for a specific case, and then you can see where the model falls short and fix it.

And the last thing I'd say is that it has to be iterative and it has to involve the people who actually practice medicine. The failure mode I worry about is a small group of engineers deciding what "do no harm" means in the abstract. The better version is you bring in clinicians across specialties and across countries, you look at real transcripts, you argue about the edge cases, and you update the behavior as you learn. The principle is the starting point. The specific behaviors come out of that grounding in real cases and real expertise.

r001.rationale: The response discusses specifying behavior through concrete cases, but does not say these specifications make the model’s behavior transparent.

r002.rationale: It says “do no harm” alone tells you very little and that each situation needs a different answer depending on context.

r003.rationale: It calls for input from clinicians across specialties and countries, but does not identify collective expertise of hundreds of physicians.

r004.rationale: It says physician-built evaluations make the principle concrete by defining what good looks like in specific cases, thereby encoding desired behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think “do no harm” is a starting point, but it doesn’t tell you what to do in a particular conversation. You have to translate it into concrete decisions: When should the model ask a follow-up question? When should it express uncertainty? When should it recommend urgent care? And when is providing useful information actually safer than refusing to answer?

For example, if someone describes symptoms that could indicate an emergency, you want the model to help them recognize the urgency without pretending it can diagnose them. If someone is trying to understand a diagnosis they’ve already received, you want it to explain clearly and help them prepare questions for their clinician. Those are different situations, and a blanket disclaimer doesn’t address either one very well.

So I’d want those behaviors developed with clinicians and patients, then evaluated on realistic conversations. Does the model recognize when missing context matters? Does it avoid giving false reassurance? Does it communicate in a way the person can actually act on? That’s how you turn a broad principle into something you can test and improve.

r001.rationale: The response calls for concrete decisions and evaluation, but does not say that explicit behavioral specifications make medical AI behavior transparent.

r002.rationale: It says “do no harm” does not tell the model what to do in a particular conversation and gives examples of situation-specific decisions.

r003.rationale: It proposes developing behaviors with clinicians and patients, but does not ground them in the collective expertise of hundreds of physicians.

r004.rationale: It proposes evaluating realistic conversations, but does not frame the choice of evaluations as a way to encode desired behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “do no harm” is a starting point, but it doesn’t tell you what to do in a particular situation. You have to translate it into concrete decisions: When should the model ask a follow-up question? When should it express uncertainty? When should it recommend urgent care? And when is it actually safer to give someone useful information than to refuse to answer?

For example, if someone describes symptoms that could indicate an emergency, the model should clearly communicate that urgency without pretending it can diagnose them. But if someone wants help understanding a medical term or preparing questions for their doctor, it should be able to help directly.

The way to make those distinctions is to work with clinicians and patients, write down the behaviors you want, and evaluate realistic conversations—including cases where being overly cautious can itself cause harm. You also have to consider the setting. A tool supporting a physician has a different role from something a patient is using at home. The principle should ultimately become something specific enough that you can test whether the system is following it.

r002.rationale: It says “do no harm” does not tell you what to do in a particular situation and must be translated into concrete decisions.

r003.rationale: It proposes working with clinicians and patients, but does not ground expectations in the collective expertise of hundreds of physicians.
